structure.title: Book One · A salon and two households
structure.text: A hostess keeps conversation about Napoleon running to schedule. Elsewhere young people arrange a ball, a name-day celebration or a future in the army. Introductions that seem numerous at first become useful when the same men leave these drawing rooms in uniform.

structure.title: Books Two–Three · The campaigns of 1805
structure.text: Andrei hopes for a moment of distinction and Nikolai Rostov longs to prove himself among his comrades. Orders travel slowly, a horse bolts and a hillside looks different from its two sides. The men's first encounters with battle give them very different things to tell the people at home.

structure.title: Books Four–Eight · The interval between invasions
structure.text: Estates, inheritances, engagements and dances absorb the same attention the generals gave their maps. Pierre tries to put a new conviction into practice on his land. Natasha can alter the whole course of an evening in the time it takes to sing a song.

structure.title: Books Nine–Fifteen · 1812 · An army comes to Moscow
structure.text: As the invasion reaches places the reader knows as homes, a family's decisions about horses, carts and furniture acquire consequences for strangers. Tolstoy sets these choices beside arguments over who can claim to have directed an army, an evacuation or a retreat.

structure.title: Two epilogues
structure.text: The first follows the business of living together after years of upheaval. The second returns to the historian's difficulty. Knowing the outcome makes it easy to pick out an earlier act and confer on it a power nobody could have recognised at the time.

people.name: Pierre Bezukhov
people.text: Wealth gives Pierre the power to act on his enthusiasms before he has learnt much about their objects. His efforts to improve an estate, understand a secret society or see a battle at first hand expose just how much a sincere visitor can miss.

people.name: Andrei Bolkonsky
people.text: His father values precision and obedience. Andrei longs to distinguish himself somewhere beyond his father's house and the tedious social round. Campaign and family life keep putting that longing in the company of people who need something else from him.

people.name: Natasha Rostova
people.text: Natasha grows up among siblings, guests, music and money troubles. Her responsiveness makes her remarkably quick to sense what an evening calls for. It can also leave her at the mercy of somebody who knows how to arrange an evening.

people.name: Nikolai and Sonya
people.role: Young people in the Rostov household
people.text: The family welcomes Sonya as a dependent cousin. Her attachment to Nikolai makes the distinction between being loved as a daughter and having a daughter’s claims suddenly urgent. An engagement can look entirely different to the two people making it and to the parents who must find the money.

context.title: Russian names in company
context.text: One person may be addressed by a nickname at home, by first name and patronymic when politeness matters, and by family name on campaign. Who uses which form often says whether somebody is claiming intimacy, keeping a distance or trying to put a young officer in his place.

context.title: French at a Russian dinner
context.text: Several aristocrats speak French as comfortably as Russian. A conversation can change languages as somebody changes company or begins to speak from the heart. When Napoleon invades, the fashionable language of the drawing room also belongs to the enemy.

notice.text: Compare an order with its arrival.
notice.why: From headquarters a manoeuvre looks like a single act. Follow the messenger to a tired man on unfamiliar ground and the order changes meaning, sometimes before anyone has even misunderstood it.

The Rostovs' hospitality feels inexhaustible to a guest. A few pages spent with the person paying for dinner can give the same generosity a different colour without making the guest's pleasure any less real.

opening: Pierre inherits a fortune and discovers that everyone knows what he should do with it. Andrei goes to war hoping to escape a life that already feels wasted. Natasha is young enough to believe happiness must be just about to begin. Napoleon is approaching, but these people still have to fall in love, endure dinner parties, and decide whom to trust. Tolstoy makes their private hopes so absorbing that history arrives as it does in life, interrupting things that seemed more important.
